newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia's outgoing president urges further reform.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia's outgoing president urges further reform.

text.p: Mongolia's outgoing President Punsalmaagiin Ochirbat urged parliament in his farewell speech on Thursday to help the country stay firmly on its path towards democracy and a market-driven economy.
"I appeal ... to you to direct all your talents and collective effort to continue decisively along the path that our country has chosen," Ochirbat told the Great Hural, or parliament.
"Do not allow the foundation ... that has been erected to restore a new democratic Mongolia to be shaken, do not let the flame go down," he said.

Ochirbat, 55, ran for re-election last month on the ticket of the ruling Democratic Union Coalition but was defeated by N. Bagabandi, candidate of the formerly communist opposition Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party (MPRP).

Ochirbat had backed a drive to scrap Stalinist central planning and adopt market-style reforms, but his programme led to harsh economic dislocations such as surging inflation and mounting unemployment.

He became Mongolia's first directly elected president in 1993 when he swept to victory after being dumped by his former party the MPRP, which was then in power. He first became president in an election by parliament in 1990, after a bloodless revolution in Mongolia rejected socialism and embraced democracy.
Ochirbat told the Great Hural that Mongolia had been courageous in cutting free from seven decades of socialism.
"The country was in deep crisis ... and society was split in two," he said, referring to the time in 1990 when tensions between reformist democrats and supporters of socialism were at their height.
"The task that fell on me was to reconcile the fierce fight between the old and the new in a peaceful way," he said.
He hailed advances of the past seven years, which include the new multi-party political system and Mongolia's opening up to the outside world. "Mongolia has become an open country," he said.
Ochirbat is to hand over the presidential seal to Bagabandi at an inauguration ceremony on Friday.
Diplomats say members of the reformist government have privately expressed concern over potential difficulties with the new president, especially over ambitious reforms for land privatisation.
Mongolia's president is largely a figurehead, but has the power to block legislation.
Ochirbat's reformist coalition still controls parliament, although it is one seat short of the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto.
